data.title: Improved Peatland Management
data.short_summary:
Improved management of drained peatland soils due to partial rewetting of peatlands converted to arable lands (tropical, temperate, and boreal peatlands).

Units: all raster data (.tif) are in tCO2e/ha/yr. All tabular data (.csv) are summarised in tCO2e/yr.
data.description:
This layer shows estimated mitigation potential achieved through improved peatland management, measuring the avoided oxidation of soil carbon from rewetting of soils from a 10cm increase in the annual water table level. This value is based off an agricultural optimization scenario, where water table levels aren’t fully restored to their maximum height to ensure that food and fibre yields are not negatively impacted. 

Consistent with the naturebase accounting framework, areas of overlap between cropland and non-cropland pathway extents were resolved using a proportional allocation approach. Cropland pathway mitigation was weighted by the fraction of each 1 km² pixel classified as cropland, while non-cropland pathway mitigation was weighted by the inverse proportion. For a detailed description of this methodology, see Section I(c), Cropland Extent, in the NCS Accounting Rules Narrative.

Units: all raster data (.tif) are in tCO2e/ha/yr. All tabular data (.csv) are summarised in tCO2e/yr.

To calculate the per hectare mitigation potential (density) of the NCS implementation extent in tCO2e/ha/yr: 
1) Find the total mitigation value: this is provided in the spreadsheet as [pathway]_tco2e
2) Find the NCS hectare extent: This is provided in the spreadsheet as [pathway]_ha
3) Divide the mitigation value by the NCS hectare extent: tCO2e/ha/yr = [pathway]_tco2e / [pathway]_ha*

*FLAG: As this is the hectares of NCS extent of the 1km2 raster, extent may be over-estimated. Use with caution. These area estimates are not recommended for pathways that have extents finer than 1km resolution



To calculate the per hectare mitigation potential (density) for each administrative area* in tCO2e/ha/yr: 
1) Find the total mitigation value: this is provided in the spreadsheet as [pathway]_tco2e
2) Find the administrative extent: This is provided in the spreadsheet as 'admin_ha'
3) Divide the mitigation value by the administrative extent: tCO2e/ha/yr in each administrative area = [pathway]_tco2e / admin_ha

*This is useful for comparison between administrative areas

Please consult the download package under 'Download Now' for comprehensive metadata and a detailed description.
data.preferred_citation: Naturebase (2025, April 15). Improved Peatland Management v3. Retrieved from  https://naturebase.org
data.data_caveats: Burned area and pasturelands were not included under the improved management scenario. Annual mitigation was assumed to be consistent throughout the accounting horizon period for CO2, N2O, and CH4, with the latter having an exception in the boreal to account for the methane pulse of short-lived GHG emissions. In this case, we assumed a 12-year window in which methane emissions were significant. Furthermore, nutrient profiles in the boreal were assumed to be nutrient-poor, as there is not geospatial information distinguishing nutrient-poor peatlands from nutrient-rich.
data.authors: Samantha Yeo, Nisa Novita, Adibtya Asyhari, Rasis Putra Ritonga, Adi Gangga, Chris Zganjar, Peter Ellis
data.approach_and_methods:
Improved peatland management measures the avoided emissions from a 10cm increase in the annual water table level. This value is based off an agricultural optimization scenario, where water table levels aren’t fully restored to their maximum height to ensure that food and fibre yields are not negatively impacted. The total potential was estimated by calculating the total extent of drained peatlands overlapping the Map of Agreement on Global Cropland (Tubiello et al. 2022). This dataset was resampled to indicate the proportion of each 1km pixel that is mapped as cropland in at least 3 (of 6) global products in 2020 at the 30m pixel scale. To determine the extent of degraded peatlands we used the intersection of FAO Annual Drained Organic Soils for the year 2018 in Croplands and Grasslands (Conchedda & Tubiello, 2020) and Global Peatland Extent (Xu et al., 2018), with regional peatland datasets used in Angola* (Lourenco et al., in preparation), Argentina (Sayre et al., 2008), Chile (Environmental Ministry, 2020), and Mongolia (Minayeva et al., 2004). The World Ecosystems dataset (Sayre et al., 2020), derived from the FAO Global Ecological Zones, was used to distinguish climatic and landcover types. Lesiv et al. (2022) Global Forest Management Data was used to distinguish agroforestry and plantations (including oil palm). All raster datasets were rescaled to 1km2 resolution. Emissions factors from the IPCC Wetlands Supplement (2014) were applied for CO2, CH4, and N2O from tables 2.1, 2.3, and 2.5, respectively (IPCC, 2014). Of the emissions, it was assumed that rewetting would reduce them by 62% and 74% in boreal croplands and grasslands, 62% and 75% in temperate croplands and grasslands, 63% and 76% in tropical grasslands and croplands (Evans et al., 2021), and 31% in tropical oil palm plantations (Novita et al., 2024) compared to the initial conditions. 

*For Angola peatland extent, the data in the publication outputs a probability of peatland surface from 0-100. Extent was filtered for probability of greater than or equal to 50%.
data.additionality: We applied additional spatially explicit filters to avoid double-counting when applying emissions.

data.title: Peatland Restoration
data.short_summary:
Restorable emissions of soil carbon (CO2 and CH4) due to soil re-wetting in tropical, temperate, and boreal peatlands.

Units: all raster data (.tif) are in tCO2e/ha/yr. All tabular data (.csv) are summarised in tCO2e/yr.
data.description:
This layer shows estimated peatland restoration potential, measuring the avoided oxidation of soil carbon from rewetting of soils.  

Peatland restoration potential was estimated by calculating the total extent of converted peatlands and applying emissions to this degraded area for various land uses and climatic zones outside of croplands. To determine the extent of degraded peatlands we used the intersection of FAO Annual Drained Organic Soils for the year 2018 in Croplands and Grasslands (Conchedda & Tubiello, 2020) and Global Peatland Extent (Xu et al., 2018). Emissions factors from the IPCC Wetlands Supplement (2014) were applied for CO2, CH4, and N2O from tables 2.1, 2.3, and 2.5, respectively (IPCC, 2014). Of these emissions, it was assumed that rewetting would reduce them by 50% compared to the initial conditions (Griscom et al., 2017). 

Consistent with the naturebase accounting framework, areas of overlap between cropland and non-cropland pathway extents were resolved using a proportional allocation approach. Cropland pathway mitigation was weighted by the fraction of each 1 km² pixel classified as cropland, while non-cropland pathway mitigation was weighted by the inverse proportion. For a detailed description of this methodology, see Section I(c), Cropland Extent, in the NCS Accounting Rules Narrative.

Units: all raster data (.tif) are in tCO2e/ha/yr. All tabular data (.csv) are summarised in tCO2e/yr.

To calculate the per hectare mitigation potential (density) of the NCS implementation extent in tCO2e/ha/yr: 
1) Find the total mitigation value: this is provided in the spreadsheet as [pathway]_tco2e
2) Find the NCS hectare extent: This is provided in the spreadsheet as [pathway]_ha
3) Divide the mitigation value by the NCS hectare extent: tCO2e/ha/yr = [pathway]_tco2e / [pathway]_ha*

*FLAG: As this is the hectares of NCS extent of the 1km2 raster, extent may be over-estimated. Use with caution. These area estimates are not recommended for pathways that have extents finer than 1km resolution

1) Find the total mitigation value: this is provided in the spreadsheet as [pathway]_tco2e
2) Find the administrative extent: This is provided in the spreadsheet as 'admin_ha'
3) Divide the mitigation value by the administrative extent: tCO2e/ha/yr in each administrative area = [pathway]_tco2e / admin_ha

*This is useful for comparison between administrative areas

data.preferred_citation: Naturebase (2025, April 15). Peatland Restoration Potential v3. Retrieved from  https://naturebase.org
data.data_caveats: We assume degraded wetlands have already lost 50% of their original carbon stocks, reasoning that the global aggregate of degraded wetlands represents a balanced chronosequence of all phases of carbon depletion. Annual mitigation was assumed to be consistent throughout the accounting horizon period for CO2, N2O, and CH4, with the latter having an exception in the boreal to account for the methane pulse of short-lived GHG emissions. In this case, we assumed a 12-year window in which methane emissions were significant. Furthermore, nutrient profiles in the boreal were assumed to be nutrient-poor, as there is not geospatial information distinguishing nutrient-poor peatlands from nutrient-rich.
data.authors: Samantha Yeo, Nisa Novita, Adibtya Asyhari, Rasis Putra Ritonga, Adi Gangga, Chris Zganjar, Peter Ellis
data.approach_and_methods:
Peatland restoration potential measures the avoided oxidation of soil carbon from rewetting. Peatland restoration potential was estimated by calculating the total extent of drained peatlands and applying emissions to this degraded area for various land uses and climatic zones. To determine the extent of degraded peatlands we used the intersection of FAO Annual Drained Organic Soils for the year 2018 in Croplands and Grasslands (Conchedda & Tubiello, 2020) and Global Peatland Extent (Xu et al., 2018), with exceptions for: Angola* (Lourenco et al., in preparation), Argentina (Sayre et al., 2008), Chile (Environmental Ministry, 2020), and Mongolia (Minayeva et al., 2004) where regional datasets were used. The World Ecosystems dataset (Sayre et al., 2020), derived from the FAO Global Ecological Zones, was used to distinguish climatic and landcover types. We excluded cropland extent using the 2020 Cropland Agreement map (Tubiello et al. 2022). This dataset was resampled to indicate the proportion of each 1km pixel that is mapped as cropland in at least 3 (of 6) global products in 2020 at the 30m pixel scale. This multiplier was then applied to the mitigation of the pathway, to reduce the impact of croplands proportionately in each pixel. All raster datasets were rescaled to 1km2 resolution 

Emissions factors from the IPCC Wetlands Supplement (2014) were applied for CO2, CH4, and N2O from tables 2.1, 2.3, and 2.5, respectively (IPCC, 2014).  

To calculate fire emissions, we used Equation 2.8 in the 2013 Supplement to the 2006 IPCC Guidelines for national greenhouse gas inventories for both CO2 and CH4 (IPCC, 2014). In the equation, the Gef variable was supplemented for CO2 and CH4 with values from table 2.7 of Yokelson et al. 2022, and the Cf (combustion factor) was derived from Krisnawati et al. (2021). For MB (mass of fuel available for combustion) values were obtained from table 2.6 of the IPCC (2014) supplement, with the assumed sub-category wildfire as there is no geospatial information for prescribed burns. MODIS Monthly Burned Area (Giglio et al., 2021) data was used to calculate total annual burn extent in hectares for the years 2013-2022, masking pixels with over 10% level of uncertainty. A ten-year period was chosen in order to provide a sufficient average area for burned extent. From here, a fractional multiplier for the average extent of hectares burned per pixel over the last 10 years was applied to the emissions factors. In order to avoid double counting, the emissions from fire were used over the emissions from converted and drained peatlands, where they overlapped. Of the emissions, it was assumed that rewetting would reduce them by 50% compared to the initial conditions. 

 *For Angola peatland extent, the data in the publication outputs a probability of peatland surface from 0-100. Extent was filtered for probability of greater than or equal to 50%.
data.additionality: We applied additional spatially explicit filters to avoid double-counting when applying emissions.
